extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/aesthetics (readers of Schopenhauer)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the philosophical criteria Schopenhauer gives for what distinguishes genius from the ordinary intellect or talent: its source (perception), its relation to will, temperament, strengths and disadvantages, and the social/temporal consequences of its activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominance of intellect over will
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius consists in the knowing faculty receiving a considerably greater development than the service of the will; roughly the normal man is two‑thirds will and one‑third intellect, the genius the reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer uses this as a defining metric: an 'abnormally large measure of intellect' that emancipates itself from the will (a chemical simile is offered). Evaluate persons by the relative preponderance of reflective, objective knowledge versus will‑directed, practical concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary manifestation in perceptive originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The first manifestation of a surplus of knowledge-power shows itself primarily in original and fundamental knowledge of perception, occasioning repetition in an image — hence the painter and sculptor as direct examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine productions in every art receive their spark from perceptive apprehension; assess creative work for its rootedness in vivid, original perceptive images rather than mere conceptual manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as an indispensable tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination is required to complete, arrange, retain, and repeat perceptive pictures at will; only by imagination can genius call up the objects/events in lively images tailored to artistic or philosophical needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for creative power to summon and recombine percepts (the ability 'to call up spirits' at the right time). Works showing flexible, vivid imaginative recomposition of perception indicate this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeing the universal in the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Always to see the universal in the particular is the fundamental characteristic of genius; the normal man perceives particulars only as particulars (relations to his will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge thought or artwork by its degree of abstraction from mere particulars toward the universal or 'Ideas' — i.e., whether the work reveals the general, essential forms behind particular appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflectiveness / freedom of intellect from will
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius attains moments when the intellect is freed from its service to the will (the 'pure subject' of knowledge), producing objective, painlessly serene knowledge; these moments are inspiration or initiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify states or products arising from 'intellect delivered from the jurisdiction of the will' — spontaneity, necessity rather than intentional calculation. Anti‑pattern: work motivated by personal aims or calculation rather than this sort of freed reflectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productions proceed from instinctive necessity, not intentional choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of genius do not proceed from intention or choice but are guided by an instinctive necessity — the 'awaking of genius' is attainment of intellectual freedom, not deliberate planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work's form/force feels necessary and organic rather than contrived or opportunistic; deliberate pandering to audience or personal advancement indicates the opposite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works are 'useless' (autotelic) — art for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: The works of genius serve no useful ends (they are 'nothing to use'); their 'patent of nobility' is purposelessness in the practical sense — they exist for their own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between creations aimed at utility or contemporaneous needs (talent) and those created as ends in themselves; value placed on purposeless beauty and truth signals genius‑type production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of creation: perception & image vs conceptions/abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine works of genius spring from perceptive apprehension and image; by contrast, works of mere talent arise from conceptions and abstractions and serve present practical needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an artistic or philosophical product, check whether it originates in vivid perceptual insight and images (genius) or in abstracted, calculated reasoning (talent). Examples: sculpture/painting (perception) vs calculative/mathematical achievements (talent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective seriousness (not personal good will)
rubrics_metrics.description: True seriousness that characterises genius lies not in personal, practical aims or 'good will' but in an 'objective' seriousness directed outside the individual's own welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the motive: if the agent seeks objective/theoretical ends (even at personal cost) this indicates genius; if action is guided by personal advancement or moral good will to promote personal welfare, it is not the genius‑type seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melancholy temperament often accompanies genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is commonly accompanied by melancholy; the brighter the intellect, the more distinctly it perceives the misery of its condition, producing a temperament often observed in great minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperamental markers (frequent melancholy, moments of serene objectivity amid sadness) support the identification of genius. Historical/literary exempla (Goethe, Mont Blanc image) are used as illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyper‑sensibility, emotional extravagance, and lack of soberness
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of heightened intellectual power, genius often exhibits hyper‑sensibility, vehemence, passionate changes of mood, and a lack of soberness (seeing more in things than belongs to them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate behavioral and affective signs: disproportionate emotional reactions to trivial stimuli, quick shifts between absence and passion, and exaggeration of appearances point to this criterion; conversely, 'soberness' signals non‑genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme concentration leading to both achievement and overreaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius concentrates all mental forces intensely on a point, which produces great theoretical achievements but can also magnify trivial things into monstrous significance (the 'flea under the solar microscope').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for monomaniacal focus in creative efforts as a double‑edged sign: a source of breakthroughs and of disproportionate responses in ordinary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social solitude and difficulty thinking 'in common'
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius lives essentially alone: too rare and different to be companionable; its pace and interests make conversation and communal thought uncomfortable for both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess social patterns: preference for solitude, limited friendships, greater pleasure in the company of equals (often only via their works) indicate this feature; failure to integrate socially is a typical disadvantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical disadvantages and unsuitability for ordinary life
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the genius' intellect frequently abandons service of the will, the individual may be impractical, unable to further personal welfare, and sometimes appear mad or useless in daily conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging life outcomes, recognize that genius often entails poor management of personal affairs, economic hardship, and eccentric behavior — these are not evidence against the work's value but common accompanying disadvantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal incongruity with contemporaneous taste (ahead of the age)
rubrics_metrics.description: The genius does not fit the age's regular cultural progress; his works are thrown 'far out' in front, and recognition often comes only with posterity, whereas men of talent match their era and are immediately appreciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reception history: works that transcend contemporary comprehension or are valued primarily by later generations fit this criterion; immediate popularity tends to indicate talent rather than true genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between capacity for deeds and for works
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a basic distinction: 'deeds' (practical action) require an intellect continually in the service of the will (presence of mind, decision), while 'works' (art, philosophy) require objectivity and depth of knowledge coming from intellect freed from will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify achievements by whether they are practical accomplishments requiring timely decision and applied intellect (deeds) or enduring creative/theoretical productions requiring detached, objective reflection (works).
